mainEntity.name: What is the difference between cybersecurity and cyber resilience?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cybersecurity aims to prevent compromise. Cyber resilience assumes some attacks will succeed and focuses on continuing critical operations and recovering quickly.

mainEntity.name: How should a board oversee cyber risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: By setting risk appetite, receiving reporting in business terms, testing incident readiness and ensuring accountability is clear between management and the board.

mainEntity.name: What is a cybersecurity maturity assessment?

acceptedAnswer.text: A structured review of governance, controls and capabilities against a recognized framework, showing current maturity, gaps and a prioritized improvement plan.

mainEntity.name: How does AI change cybersecurity?

acceptedAnswer.text: AI creates new assets to protect, new attack techniques for adversaries and new tools for defenders. All three need to be in the security strategy.

mainEntity.name: Where should we start with enterprise AI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with a decision or process where value is measurable, data exists and the risk is manageable. A focused first use case builds both evidence and governance muscle.

mainEntity.name: What is AI governance?

acceptedAnswer.text: AI governance is the set of policies, roles, controls and oversight that ensure AI systems are used safely, lawfully and in line with business objectives across their lifecycle.

mainEntity.name: How do you keep sensitive data secure when using generative AI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Through data classification, architecture choices such as private or in-region deployment, access controls and output monitoring, decided before any model sees sensitive data.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between AI automation and AI agents?

acceptedAnswer.text: Automation executes a defined task. An agent pursues a goal across steps and systems, choosing actions within limits, so it needs stronger permissions design and oversight.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between climate risk and ESG?

acceptedAnswer.text: ESG is a broad set of environmental, social and governance factors. Climate risk is a specific financial risk: the physical and transition impacts of climate change on an organization's value.

mainEntity.name: What are physical and transition risks?

acceptedAnswer.text: Physical risks come from climate hazards such as heat, flooding or water stress. Transition risks come from the shift to a low-carbon economy: policy, carbon pricing, technology and market changes.

mainEntity.name: What are financed emissions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Financed emissions are the greenhouse gas emissions associated with a financial institution's loans and investments. They are usually the largest part of a bank's or investor's footprint.

mainEntity.name: Why connect climate to enterprise risk management?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because climate risk shows up through existing risk types such as credit, operational, market and reputational risk. Managed separately, its effects are underestimated.

mainEntity.name: What is AI governance for boards?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the board's role in setting AI risk appetite, assigning accountability, obtaining assurance and keeping AI oversight current. Management runs AI governance; the board ensures it is effective.

mainEntity.name: Is AI governance a legal requirement for boards?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some sectors and jurisdictions, yes. Qatar's central bank, for example, places AI accountability with the boards of licensed entities. Elsewhere it is increasingly a fiduciary expectation.

mainEntity.name: What is an AI register?

acceptedAnswer.text: An AI register is an inventory of every AI system an organization uses, recording its purpose, owner, risk level, data, vendor and controls.

mainEntity.name: Does the EU AI Act apply to companies in the GCC?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can. The Act applies to providers placing AI on the EU market and to deployers whose AI outputs are used in the EU, regardless of where they are based.

mainEntity.name: When do EU AI Act high-risk obligations apply?

acceptedAnswer.text: For stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III, from 2 December 2027, following the Digital Omnibus. Transparency obligations under Article 50 have applied since 2 August 2026.

mainEntity.name: What is ISO/IEC 42001?

acceptedAnswer.text: ISO/IEC 42001 is the international standard for AI management systems, setting requirements for establishing, operating and improving AI governance within an organization.

mainEntity.name: What is a cyber resilience strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: A cyber resilience strategy is a plan to keep critical services running and recover quickly from cyber attacks, combining prioritization, protection, testing and recovery.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between cybersecurity and cyber resilience?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cybersecurity aims to prevent attacks. Cyber resilience assumes some will succeed and focuses on continuing operations and recovering.

mainEntity.name: What is the Minimum Viable Enterprise?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the smallest set of services, systems, data and people an organization needs to keep operating through a severe incident, used to prioritize resilience investment.

mainEntity.name: How should boards measure cyber resilience?

acceptedAnswer.text: With outcome metrics such as tested recovery times for critical services, time to contain incidents, supplier fallbacks and the results of crisis exercises.

mainEntity.name: What is NIST CSF 2.0's Govern function?

acceptedAnswer.text: Govern is the function added in NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 that covers cyber risk strategy, roles, policy and oversight within enterprise risk management.

mainEntity.name: Is the NIA standard mandatory in Qatar?

acceptedAnswer.text: The National Information Assurance standard is mandatory for government entities and critical infrastructure operators in Qatar and is maintained by the National Cyber Security Agency. Other organizations often adopt it as best practice.

jsonLd.headline: Integrated Risk Management: Seeing the Risks Between Your Risk Registers
jsonLd.description: Integrated risk management connects cyber, technology, third-party and operational risk so leaders see combined exposure. A practical model for executives.

mainEntity.name: What is integrated risk management?

acceptedAnswer.text: Integrated risk management brings risk domains such as cyber, technology, operational and third-party risk into one framework, data model and decision process, so combined exposures are visible.

mainEntity.name: How is IRM different from GRC?

acceptedAnswer.text: GRC focuses on documenting risks, controls and compliance. IRM focuses on how risks connect and what decisions they require, using continuous data and scenarios.

mainEntity.name: Is integrated risk management the same as ERM?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Enterprise risk management is the overall discipline and framework. IRM is the practical integration of risk data, processes and technology that lets ERM work across domains.

mainEntity.name: What is risk aggregation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk aggregation is the combining of individual risks to understand total or combined exposure, accounting for dependencies rather than simply adding scores.

mainEntity.name: Where should an organization start with IRM?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a common risk taxonomy and a map of important business services, linked to the assets and suppliers they depend on.

mainEntity.name: Can risk be quantified in IRM?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, using scenarios and models that produce ranges. Where data is thin, stated confidence levels keep quantification honest.

jsonLd.headline: Climate Risk Management in Banking: From Disclosure to Decision
jsonLd.description: Climate risk management in banking now spans IFRS S2, PCAF financed emissions and stress testing. What GCC and global bank leaders need to decide next.

mainEntity.name: What is climate risk management in banking?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is the identification, measurement, monitoring and control of financial risks from climate change, integrated into credit, market, operational and strategic risk management.

mainEntity.name: What are financed emissions?

acceptedAnswer.text: Financed emissions are greenhouse gas emissions attributable to a financial institution's loans and investments. They fall under Scope 3, Category 15 of the GHG Protocol.

mainEntity.name: What is the PCAF standard?

acceptedAnswer.text: PCAF's Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard sets methods for financial institutions to measure financed, facilitated and insurance-associated emissions. Part A, on financed emissions, reached its third edition in December 2025.

mainEntity.name: Is IFRS S2 mandatory for banks in Qatar?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. QCB-regulated banks and insurers must report under IFRS S1 and S2 for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026, with first reports in 2027.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between physical and transition risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Physical risk comes from climate hazards such as heat, flooding and water stress. Transition risk comes from policy, technology and market shifts toward a lower-carbon economy.

mainEntity.name: What is a PCAF data quality score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A score from 1 to 5 indicating the reliability of emissions data used for each exposure, from verified reported emissions (1) to broad estimates (5).
